main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the structure of the Earth
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the origin and the structure of the Earth and earth systems
learning_activity_name: Explain the concept and scope of Geography (branches, importance and relationship with other disciplines)
sla_name: Meaning, Branches and Scope of Geography
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly define Geography and list its main branches with their importance.
sla_teaching_aids: Wall charts|Textbooks|Pictures of physical and human landscapes|Marker pens
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Geography is the science that studies the Earth's surface, the physical features found on it, and the relationship between people and their environment. It has two broad branches: physical geography and human geography.
sla_notes_details: Physical geography studies natural features such as landforms, climate, soils and vegetation, while human geography studies population, settlements, economic activities and their interaction with the environment. Geography borrows from and relates to other disciplines such as geology, biology, economics and sociology, making it an integrating subject. Studying Geography helps learners understand how natural processes and human activities shape the world around them.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a geographer studying Mount Kilimanjaro examines its physical formation (physical geography) as well as the tourism and farming activities of communities living around it (human geography).
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowledge of Geography helps people understand weather patterns, choose suitable land for farming or settlement, and manage natural resources wisely.
sla_exercise: Define Geography.::Geography is the study of the Earth's surface, its physical features, and the relationship between people and their environment.||State the two main branches of Geography.::Physical geography and human geography.||Name one discipline related to Geography.::Geology (also acceptable: biology, economics, or sociology).

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the structure of the Earth
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the origin and the structure of the Earth and earth systems
learning_activity_name: Describe the Earth (origin, shape, size, position and movements of the earth in the solar system, and parallels and meridians)
sla_name: Origin, Shape and Movements of the Earth
sla_assessment_criteria: Students accurately describe the origin, shape, position and movements of the Earth, and locate places using parallels and meridians.
sla_teaching_aids: Globe|Picture of the solar system|World map|Chart showing latitudes and longitudes
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The Earth is the third planet from the Sun in the solar system. According to the widely accepted nebular hypothesis, the Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a rotating cloud of gas and dust that condensed under gravity.
sla_notes_details: The Earth is almost spherical in shape, slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator, a shape called an oblate spheroid. It has two main movements: rotation, which is the spinning of the Earth on its own axis once every 24 hours causing day and night, and revolution, which is the movement of the Earth around the Sun once every 365¼ days causing the seasons. Parallels (lines of latitude) run east-west and measure distance north or south of the Equator, while meridians (lines of longitude) run north-south and measure distance east or west of the Greenwich (Prime) Meridian.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the Equator (0° latitude) passes through Kenya just north of Tanzania, while the Greenwich Meridian (0° longitude) passes through the United Kingdom; together these two lines are used as reference points for locating any place on Earth's grid system.
sla_notes_daily_life: Latitude and longitude coordinates are used daily in GPS navigation systems, in aviation, and in determining local time in different parts of the world.
sla_exercise: What causes day and night on Earth?::The rotation of the Earth on its own axis.||How long does the Earth take to revolve around the Sun?::About 365¼ days (one year).||What is the difference between a parallel and a meridian?::A parallel (latitude) runs east-west and measures north-south position, while a meridian (longitude) runs north-south and measures east-west position.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the structure of the Earth
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the major features of the Earth surface
learning_activity_name: Describe major features of the Earth's surface (continents, oceans, major relief features, large inland water bodies and vegetation zones)
sla_name: Continents, Oceans and Major Relief Features
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly identify and describe the major continents, oceans, relief features, inland water bodies and vegetation zones of the world.
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The Earth's surface is made up of large landmasses called continents and vast bodies of salt water called oceans. There are seven continents: Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Australia and Antarctica, and five oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic.
sla_notes_details: Major relief features include mountains (e.g. fold mountains and volcanic mountains), plateaus, and plains, each formed by different geological processes such as folding, faulting and volcanic activity. Large inland water bodies include lakes and inland seas, which are important sources of fresh water. Vegetation zones such as tropical rainforest, savanna, desert and tundra are distributed across the Earth largely according to climate.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Africa's Great Rift Valley contains large inland lakes such as Lake Victoria and Lake Tanganyika, and is bordered by volcanic mountains such as Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest peak.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding relief and vegetation helps farmers choose suitable crops, and helps planners decide where to build roads, settlements and dams.
sla_exercise: Name the seven continents of the world.::Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Australia and Antarctica.||Give one example of a large inland water body in East Africa.::Lake Victoria (also acceptable: Lake Tanganyika).||What is a plateau?::A plateau is a raised, mostly flat area of land higher than the surrounding land.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the structure of the Earth
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the origin and the structure of the Earth and earth systems
learning_activity_name: Describe the internal structure of the Earth (crust, mantle, core) and their major characteristics (location, size/thickness, density and gross composition)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly describe the crust, mantle and core, and state their location, thickness, density and composition.
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The Earth is made up of three main internal layers: the crust, the mantle and the core. Each layer differs in thickness, density and composition.
sla_notes_details: The crust is the thin, outermost solid layer on which we live, made of light rocks and averaging about 5 to 70 kilometres thick. The mantle lies below the crust, is about 2,900 kilometres thick, and is made of dense, semi-molten silicate rock. The core is the innermost layer, made mostly of iron and nickel; it is divided into a liquid outer core and a solid inner core, and is the densest layer due to immense pressure and heat.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, molten rock (magma) that reaches the Earth's surface through volcanoes such as Ol Doinyo Lengai in Tanzania originates from partially melted material in the upper mantle.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding the Earth's internal structure helps explain natural events such as volcanic eruptions and earthquakes, which affect where people can safely settle and build.
sla_exercise: Name the three main internal layers of the Earth.::The crust, the mantle and the core.||Which layer of the Earth is the thinnest?::The crust.||What are the two main minerals that make up the Earth's core?::Iron and nickel.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the structure of the Earth
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the origin and the structure of the Earth and earth systems
learning_activity_name: Describe the main external Earth systems (Hydrosphere, Atmosphere and Biosphere)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly describe the hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere and give examples of each.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts|World map|Pictures of water bodies, air layers and living organisms
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Besides its internal layers, the Earth has external systems that support life: the hydrosphere, the atmosphere and the biosphere.
sla_notes_details: The hydrosphere consists of all the water on Earth, including oceans, lakes, rivers, groundwater and ice. The atmosphere is the layer of gases, mainly nitrogen and oxygen, that surrounds the Earth and protects it while enabling weather and climate. The biosphere is the zone where all living organisms, including plants, animals and humans, exist and interact with the hydrosphere and atmosphere.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Lake Victoria (hydrosphere) supports fish and other aquatic life (biosphere), while evaporation from the lake contributes moisture to the surrounding atmosphere, influencing local rainfall.
sla_notes_daily_life: These three systems interact to determine the weather, water supply and food production that people depend on every day.
sla_exercise: What does the hydrosphere consist of?::All the water on Earth, including oceans, lakes, rivers, groundwater and ice.||Which two gases make up most of the atmosphere?::Nitrogen and oxygen.||What is the biosphere?::The zone of the Earth where all living organisms exist and interact.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills and techniques in Geography
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the basic techniques of map and photograph interpretation
learning_activity_name: Describe the basic principles of reading and interpreting maps (key, symbols, direction, margin/frame, map title, scale and contour patterns)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly identify and explain the key, symbols, direction, margin, title, scale and contour patterns on a map.
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A map is a scaled representation of part of the Earth's surface drawn on a flat sheet of paper. Reading a map correctly requires understanding its basic elements.
sla_notes_details: These elements include the key or legend, which explains the symbols used; symbols, which represent real features such as roads and rivers; direction, usually shown by a north arrow; the margin or frame, which borders the map; the map title, which tells what the map shows; the scale, which relates map distance to ground distance; and contour patterns, which are lines joining points of equal height and show the shape of the land.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, closely spaced contour lines on a topographical map of the Uluguru Mountains indicate steep slopes, while widely spaced contours indicate a gentle slope.
sla_notes_daily_life: Map reading skills help people navigate to new places, plan travel routes, and locate services such as schools, hospitals and markets.
sla_exercise: What is a map key or legend used for?::It explains the meaning of the symbols used on a map.||What do closely spaced contour lines indicate?::A steep slope.||What is map scale?::The relationship between distance on the map and the actual distance on the ground.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills and techniques in Geography
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the basic techniques of map and photograph interpretation
learning_activity_name: Reading and interpreting various type of maps and their importance (topographical and statistical map)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students distinguish between topographical and statistical maps and explain the importance of each.
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Maps are classified into different types based on the information they show. Two common types are topographical maps and statistical maps.
sla_notes_details: A topographical map shows the natural and human features of an area, including relief, drainage, vegetation, roads and settlements, using contour lines and symbols. A statistical map presents numerical data, such as population or rainfall distribution, using methods like dots, shading (choropleth) or graphs placed on a map base. Both types help users visualise spatial patterns that would be hard to understand from text alone.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a topographical map of the Kilimanjaro region shows its relief and rivers, while a statistical (choropleth) map of Tanzania can show population density by region using different shades of colour.
sla_notes_daily_life: Statistical maps help government planners decide where to build schools and hospitals based on population distribution, while topographical maps help engineers plan roads and dams.
sla_exercise: What does a topographical map show?::The natural and human features of an area, such as relief, drainage, vegetation and settlements.||What does a statistical map show?::Numerical data, such as population or rainfall, distributed over an area.||Give one method used to show data on a statistical map.::Choropleth shading (also acceptable: dots or graphs).

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills and techniques in Geography
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the basic techniques of map and photograph interpretation
learning_activity_name: Describe the basic concept of photograph in Geography (meaning, types, elements and uses)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly explain the meaning, types, elements and uses of photographs in Geography.
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: In Geography, a photograph is a pictorial record of part of the Earth's surface taken from the ground or from the air, used to study landscape and human activities.
sla_notes_details: There are three main types of photographs: ground photographs, taken at eye level from the ground; vertical (aerial) photographs, taken directly from above; and oblique photographs, taken from the air at an angle. Every photograph has elements such as the foreground, middle ground and background. Photographs are used in Geography to study land use, settlement patterns, vegetation cover and landform features.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a vertical aerial photograph of Dar es Salaam can be used to study the pattern of roads, buildings and the harbour from directly above.
sla_notes_daily_life: Photographs, including satellite images used in phones and maps applications, help people and planners monitor changes in towns, farms and forests over time.
sla_exercise: What is a photograph in Geography?::A pictorial record of part of the Earth's surface taken from the ground or from the air.||Name the three main types of photographs.::Ground, vertical (aerial) and oblique photographs.||Give one use of photographs in Geography.::To study land use, settlement patterns or vegetation cover (any reasonable use).

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills and techniques in Geography
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the basic techniques of map and photograph interpretation
learning_activity_name: Describe the basic principles of photograph interpretation (identifying foreground, middle ground and background, associating objects with geographical phenomena)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly identify the foreground, middle ground and background of a photograph and associate objects in it with geographical phenomena.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample ground and aerial photographs|Magnifying glass|Worksheets
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Photograph interpretation is the skill of identifying and explaining features shown in a photograph in relation to geographical processes and human activities.
sla_notes_details: A photograph is normally divided into three parts for interpretation: the foreground, which is the area nearest to the camera; the middle ground, the area beyond the foreground; and the background, the area farthest away, often near the horizon. Interpreting a photograph involves identifying physical features (such as hills, rivers or vegetation) and human features (such as roads, buildings or farms) in each part and explaining the geographical processes that produced them.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in a photograph of a farming village, the foreground may show cultivated fields, the middle ground may show houses and a road, and the background may show hills covered with forest.
sla_notes_daily_life: Photograph interpretation skills are used by land surveyors, urban planners and environmental officers to assess land use and monitor environmental change.
sla_exercise: What is the foreground of a photograph?::The area of the photograph nearest to the camera.||Why is the background of a photograph important in interpretation?::It shows features farthest from the camera, often near the horizon, helping to understand the wider landscape.||Give one human feature that can be identified in a photograph.::A road (also acceptable: buildings, farms, bridges).

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the structure of the Earth
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the relationship between relief, climate and natural vegetation
learning_activity_name: Describe the major climatic regions of the world (tropical, temperate, polar and sub-tropical)
sla_name: Major Climatic Regions of the World
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly describe the characteristics and location of the tropical, sub-tropical, temperate and polar climatic regions.
sla_teaching_aids: World climate map|Charts|Graphs of temperature and rainfall
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A climatic region is a large area of the Earth that experiences similar weather conditions of temperature and rainfall over a long period. The world is divided into major climatic regions.
sla_notes_details: The tropical region lies near the Equator and has high temperatures and heavy rainfall throughout the year. The sub-tropical region lies just outside the tropics and often has hot, dry summers. The temperate region lies in the middle latitudes and experiences four distinct seasons with moderate temperatures. The polar region lies near the poles and has extremely low temperatures with little precipitation, mostly falling as snow.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Tanzania lies within the tropical climatic region, experiencing generally high temperatures and distinct wet and dry seasons, unlike countries such as the United Kingdom which lie in the temperate region with four seasons.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowledge of climatic regions helps farmers select suitable crops and helps people plan clothing, housing and travel according to expected weather.
sla_exercise: Which climatic region does Tanzania mainly belong to?::The tropical climatic region.||What is a key characteristic of the polar climatic region?::Extremely low temperatures with little precipitation, mostly as snow.||How many main seasons does the temperate region typically experience?::Four seasons.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the structure of the Earth
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the relationship between relief, climate and natural vegetation
learning_activity_name: Describe the relationship between major features of the Earth's surface, climate, and natural vegetation
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly explain how relief and climate influence the distribution of natural vegetation.
sla_teaching_aids: Relief map|Vegetation map|Pictures of different vegetation types
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The relief (shape and height of land) and the climate of an area strongly influence the type of natural vegetation that grows there.
sla_notes_details: Areas of high altitude are generally cooler and wetter, favouring montane forest, while low-lying areas with high temperature and rainfall favour tropical rainforest. Areas with moderate rainfall and a long dry season favour savanna grassland with scattered trees, while areas with very low rainfall favour desert vegetation. Mountains can also create rain shadow effects, where one side receives heavy rainfall and dense vegetation while the leeward side remains dry with sparse vegetation.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Mount Kilimanjaro shows vegetation zones changing with altitude, from savanna at the base, through montane forest, to alpine desert and permanent snow near the summit.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding this relationship helps farmers and foresters choose appropriate crops or trees for a given altitude and climate.
sla_exercise: How does altitude affect vegetation on a mountain?::Higher altitudes are generally cooler and wetter, favouring montane forest, while lower altitudes favour savanna or forest depending on rainfall.||What is a rain shadow?::A dry area on the leeward side of a mountain that receives little rainfall because moist winds drop their rain on the windward side.||Name one vegetation zone found on Mount Kilimanjaro.::Montane forest (also acceptable: savanna, alpine desert).

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills and techniques in Geography
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the basic techniques in land surveying
learning_activity_name: Explore the basic tenets of surveying (meaning, types, equipment, methods, and importance)
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly explain the meaning, types, equipment, methods and importance of land surveying.
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Land surveying is the process of measuring and mapping the position, distance and shape of features on the Earth's surface.
sla_notes_details: There are different types of surveying, including chain/tape surveying, compass surveying and leveling, each suited to different purposes. Common equipment includes a tape measure or chain, ranging poles, pegs, an arrow and a notebook for recording measurements. Surveying methods generally involve measuring straight lines between fixed points and recording offsets to nearby features. Surveying is important for planning construction, dividing land into plots, and preparing accurate maps.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, before building a school, surveyors use chain surveying to measure and mark the exact boundaries and dimensions of the plot of land.
sla_notes_daily_life: Land surveying is used daily by land officers to demarcate plots for housing, farming and infrastructure development, helping to prevent land disputes.
sla_exercise: What is land surveying?::The process of measuring and mapping the position, distance and shape of features on the Earth's surface.||Name two pieces of equipment used in chain surveying.::Tape measure/chain and ranging poles (also acceptable: pegs, arrows).||Give one importance of land surveying.::It helps in planning construction and dividing land into plots accurately (any reasonable importance).

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic skills and techniques in Geography
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the basic techniques in land surveying
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly carry out a simple tape or chain survey of a small plot of land and record accurate measurements.
sla_teaching_aids: Tape measure or chain|Ranging poles|Pegs|Arrows|Field notebook
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Tape and chain surveying is a simple method of measuring land using a tape measure or chain, ranging poles and pegs to determine distances between points.
sla_notes_details: The process begins by fixing ranging poles at the corners of the area to be surveyed to establish straight survey lines. The surveyor then measures the distance along each line using the tape or chain, recording the measurements in a field notebook, often as a sketch called a field book diagram. Offsets, which are short measurements at right angles from the main survey line, are taken to record the position of nearby features such as trees or buildings.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, students can survey the boundary of their school compound by ranging poles at each corner and measuring each side with a tape measure, then drawing a scaled plan from the recorded measurements.
sla_notes_daily_life: This simple surveying skill can be used by farmers and community members to measure and record the size of their farms or plots of land.
sla_exercise: What equipment is used to mark straight lines in tape/chain surveying?::Ranging poles.||What is an offset in surveying?::A short measurement taken at right angles from the main survey line to record the position of a nearby feature.||Where are the measurements recorded during a survey?::In a field notebook (field book).

specific_competence_name: Carry out a project in Geography
learning_activity_name: Develop and carry out a simple research project in Geography
sla_assessment_criteria: Students in groups develop a clear research title and successfully carry out a simple field-based research project in Geography.
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A research project in Geography is a planned investigation into a real geographical problem or issue found in the local environment or community.
sla_notes_details: Developing a research project starts with choosing a clear and researchable title, such as a local land use, environmental or population issue. The student then sets simple objectives, decides on methods of data collection such as observation, interviews or questionnaires, and plans a schedule for fieldwork. During the fieldwork stage, the student collects data from key informants and through direct observation, and records findings systematically for later analysis and reporting.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a group of students could choose the title 'Causes of soil erosion in our village' and collect data through observation of farmland and interviews with local farmers.
sla_notes_daily_life: Research skills learned here are useful in identifying and solving real problems in the community, such as poor waste management or water shortages.
sla_exercise: What is the first step in developing a research project?::Choosing a clear and researchable title.||Name one method of collecting data in a Geography research project.::Interviews (also acceptable: observation, questionnaires).||Why is it important to plan a schedule for fieldwork?::It helps ensure the research is completed systematically and on time.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the relationship between geography, environmental health, human settlements and economic activities
learning_activity_name: Describe the geographical factors that influence the spatial distribution of population, human settlements and economic activities (climate, soil, relief, vegetation, transport and water supply)
sla_name: Factors Influencing Population Distribution and Settlement
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly explain how climate, soil, relief, vegetation, transport and water supply influence the distribution of population, settlements and economic activities.
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The distribution of population, human settlements and economic activities across an area is influenced by several geographical factors.
sla_notes_details: Favourable climate with moderate temperature and reliable rainfall attracts dense settlement and farming, while harsh climates such as deserts discourage settlement. Fertile soils support agriculture and attract farming communities, while gentle relief such as plains is easier to build on and cultivate than steep mountains. Good transport networks such as roads and railways encourage trade and settlement growth, and reliable water supply from rivers, lakes or boreholes is essential for both domestic use and economic activities such as irrigation and industry.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the fertile volcanic soils and reliable rainfall around Mount Kilimanjaro and Mount Meru have attracted dense population and intensive farming, while the drier central plateau of Tanzania has comparatively lower population density.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding these factors helps government planners decide where to develop new towns, roads and irrigation schemes to support growing populations.
sla_exercise: Name three geographical factors that influence population distribution.::Any three of: climate, soil, relief, vegetation, transport, water supply.||Why do fertile soils attract dense population?::They support productive agriculture, providing food and livelihoods for many people.||Give one example of an area in Tanzania with high population density due to favourable factors.::The slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro/Mount Meru (any reasonable example).

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the relationship between geography, environmental health, human settlements and economic activities
learning_activity_name: Examine the impacts of population distribution on economic activities and the environment (land use and settlement patterns changes)
sla_name: Impacts of Population Distribution on Environment
sla_assessment_criteria: Students correctly explain how population distribution affects economic activities and causes changes in land use and settlement patterns.
sla_teaching_aids: Photographs of urban and rural land use|Charts|Case study reports
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The way population is distributed across an area has significant effects on economic activities and on the natural environment.
sla_notes_details: Areas of high population density often experience increased demand for land, leading to land use changes such as conversion of farmland or forest into settlement, and expansion of economic activities like trade, industry and services. This can lead to environmental problems such as deforestation, soil erosion, pollution and loss of biodiversity if not well managed. In sparsely populated areas, land may remain underutilised, while resources such as water and energy in densely populated areas can become overstretched.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, rapid population growth in Dar es Salaam has led to the expansion of informal settlements onto previously forested or wetland areas, increasing the risk of flooding and reducing green cover.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding these impacts helps communities and local governments plan sustainable land use, such as protecting wetlands and managing waste in growing towns.
sla_exercise: Give one negative environmental impact of high population density.::Deforestation (also acceptable: soil erosion, pollution, loss of biodiversity).||How can population growth change land use patterns?::It can convert farmland or forest into settlement and other economic uses.||Name one problem caused by rapid urban population growth in Tanzania.::Expansion of informal settlements/flooding risk (any reasonable example).

specific_competence_name: Carry out a project in Geography
learning_activity_name: Complete and submit a report of the project started in Form Three
sla_name: Completing and Presenting the Geography Project Report
sla_assessment_criteria: Students successfully complete, write up and submit a well-organised report of their Form Three research project on time.
sla_teaching_aids: Draft research notes|Notebook|Pen/pencil|Computer or smartphone (where available)
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Completing a research project involves organising the data collected earlier into a clear, well-structured written report.
sla_notes_details: A good project report typically includes an introduction stating the title and objectives, a description of the methods used to collect data, presentation of findings using text, tables or simple graphs, a discussion of what the findings mean, and a conclusion with recommendations. Students should also prepare to present their findings orally to the class, explaining their key results clearly and confidently.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a group that researched 'Causes of soil erosion in our village' would present their findings on the main causes observed, illustrate them with photographs or a simple chart, and recommend measures such as terracing or tree planting.
sla_notes_daily_life: The skill of organising information into a clear report and presenting it is useful in future studies, workplaces and community meetings.
sla_exercise: What should the introduction of a project report include?::The title and objectives of the research.||Why is it useful to present findings using tables or graphs?::They make the data easier to understand and compare.||What should a project report's conclusion contain?::A summary of key findings and recommendations.
